Featured project

A working AI product case study built with synthetic data. It demonstrates requirement extraction, constraint handling, intent-aware ranking, clarification, honest failure states, and evaluation against a keyword baseline.

Intent-Aware Product Discovery · V2A

From a nuanced need to an explainable shortlist

A shopper describes a situation in natural language. The experience converts it into explicit requirements, identifies unresolved decisions, ranks a 42-product synthetic headphones catalog, and explains why each result fits and where it compromises.

Open interactive demoSee evaluation

Problem

Keyword search misses the relationships between budget, context, comfort, and quality.

Product decision

Separate hard constraints from preferences, and ask one question only when its answer changes the decision.

Evidence

On 20 frozen queries, top-three relevance improved from 65% to 80% versus the baseline.

Current limitation

Rule coverage is sensitive to wording, and unsupported catalog attributes still need a clearer response.

How the evaluation works

The evaluation was designed before aggregate scoring so the product could not redefine success after seeing the results. Both approaches use the same 42-product synthetic catalog and the same explicit hard filters.

V2A · Frozen 20-query comparison
1. Freeze the questionsTwenty unique needs cover calls, travel, comfort, device switching, budget conflicts, negation, and either-or requirements.
2. Define relevanceEach query records its hard constraints, acceptable attributes, and whether the right behavior is a result, clarification, or honest no-match state.
3. Run both methodsA price-led keyword baseline and the intent-aware workflow are judged against exactly the same criteria.
4. Preserve failuresMisses become inputs to the next version. The scoring rules are not changed to erase them.

Read this as a before-and-after test of the prototype. “Before” is a simple price-led baseline. “After” adds interpretation of the shopper’s need, ranking, and a choice when the request cannot be met. These are two methods tested on the same 20 written queries, not a measured change in real shopper behavior.

Example: “I fly twice a month and want compact headphones under $250.” The simple baseline favored cheap products that missed the travel need. The intent-aware version brought compact options with stronger noise reduction into the top three. For “under $60 with top-tier noise cancellation and a great microphone,” the intent-aware version recognized that no catalog product met everything and asked which requirement mattered most.

Hard-constraint pass rate

A firm requirement is something the system should never quietly relax, such as “wired” or “under $60.” We checked whether each displayed shortlist respected those requirements, or correctly identified a conflict. 85% to 100% means three additional queries passed this check.

Top-three relevance

For each request, we wrote down what would count as an acceptable product or a correct conflict response before scoring. 65% to 80% means a useful answer appeared within the first three options for three more queries.

Mean reciprocal rank

This measures where the first acceptable product appears: first place scores 1, second place scores 0.5, and third scores about 0.33. Higher is better. 0.458 to 0.875 shows that useful products moved much closer to the top. This measure excludes the four cases where a product rank was not the right answer.

Interaction accuracy

Sometimes the right response is a shortlist; other times it is a form-factor question, a priority question, or an honest statement that the catalog cannot support the request. 70% to 80% means the system chose that response type correctly for two more queries.

Clarification recall

Eight queries were judged to need a question. The baseline asked the expected question in four; the intent-aware version did so in six. Both methods had 100% clarification precision on this small set: every question they did ask was judged useful.

What improved

The largest gain was rank position. Relevant products moved closer to the top, and impossible budget-plus-quality requests no longer produced a misleading exact recommendation.

What still fails

Two comfort phrasings remain too dependent on exact words. Bass and studio-quality requests also reveal when the runtime catalog lacks the evidence needed to make a claim.

These results demonstrate behavior on a synthetic catalog with builder-authored judgments. They are evidence for product iteration, not a claim of production accuracy or customer impact.

How I work

I use prototypes to make product judgment inspectable. Each version records its hypothesis, failure, revision, evidence, and remaining uncertainty.

Start with the decision

Define the customer choice and the information needed to improve it.

Evaluate the full chain

Test interpretation, eligibility, ordering, explanation, and clarification—not only the final list.

Keep limitations visible

Document what the evidence supports, what it does not, and what the next version must resolve.
